solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Cyclops on date is soused in volatile rye solution

indicators.note: to be soused in liquid is to be plunged right into it, so one piece goes inside another
something volatile is unstable and liable to change, so these letters will not hold their order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: one thing set on another sits beside it, so the first piece is placed right next to the second

parts.note: Cyclops is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter refers to himself as me
D is the standard abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: The setter, out on a date, gets drunk on some rye whiskey concoction.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often stand for themselves with their pseudonym, so Cyclops means the setter in the first person. 'Solution' looks like a liquid mixture, but it means an answer to a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: A remedy is a cure or fix for a problem, which is what a solution provides.

clue.text: Music game — just the environment to get crabs

definitions.text: just the environment to get crabs

parts.note: rock is a genre of music
pool is a cue game played on a table

explanation.surface: A rock gig and a game of pool make a sleazy night out where one might catch crabs.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'crabs' means pubic lice caught from a seedy encounter; in the definition it means the shore creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock pool is seawater left among shoreline stones at low tide, the habitat where small crustaceans live.

clue.text: Married Noel, lousy sexist tit

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married

indicators.note: lousy means badly made or poor, so these letters come out in a botched order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A married man called Noel turns out to be a lousy, sexist idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tit' looks like an insult for Noel, but here it is the slang word for a breast.
explanation.definitionFit: Melons is crude, sexist slang for a woman's breasts, the same body part a tit names in vulgar speech.

clue.text: Blunt at Cyclops's command

parts.note: blunt speech is direct, frank and plain
the setter Cyclops speaking of himself: Cyclops has becomes I have, contracted

explanation.surface: Someone is being blunt because the setter ordered it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cyclops's' reads as a possessive but is Cyclops has, which in the setter's own voice is I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: A directive is an official order or instruction issued by someone in authority.

clue.text: (& 15dn.) He's gate-crashed metropolitan hen bash — it's rather embarrassingly ignored

indicators.note: a gate-crasher barges into a party uninvited, so one piece pushes its way inside the rest
to bash something is to batter it out of shape, so the letters get knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
He is taken as written; the 's is he has

explanation.surface: A man has crashed a big-city hen party, which everyone politely pretends not to notice.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is a British bachelorette party. HE joins the letters of METROPOLITAN HEN and the lot is rearranged across 4 and 15.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an obvious, awkward problem that everyone present conspicuously avoids mentioning.

clue.text: Curt, Bill eaten by desperate lion, cold

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other
someone desperate is frantic and out of control, so these letters thrash into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC
C stands for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill is devoured by a starving lion, an end told in a cold, curt way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an invoice, AC.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech uses very few words, which makes it brief and abrupt, exactly as a curt remark is.

clue.text: Life agreed to drop English diarist

parts.note: pep is energy, liveliness

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: yes is the word for agreeing
E is the abbreviation for English, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone's life story agrees to leave out an English diarist.
explanation.walkthrough: YES without its E leaves YS, attached to PEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Pepys was a seventeenth-century London official famous for the private journal he kept, which records the Great Fire.

clue.text: Retentive baronet indiscriminately swallowing bullshit

indicators.note: whatever is swallowed goes inside the swallower, so one piece encloses another
doing something indiscriminately means without order or care, so these letters land in random positions

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
BS is the common abbreviation for bullshit

explanation.surface: An anally retentive aristocrat swallows any old nonsense he is told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retentive' suggests the anal-retentive personality, but here it simply means able to keep liquid soaked up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absorbent soaks up and keeps liquid, so it retains what it takes in.

clue.text: Archer's aim: prostitute, say, back inside?

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: tart is slang for a prostitute

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so these letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: A question about whether a novelist's goal is to put a sex worker back behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Jeffrey Archer, the novelist jailed for perjury in a case involving a prostitute; the definition means a bowman.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is the board with rings that a bowman shoots arrows at, the thing they aim for.

clue.text: Two articles about three consecutive letters for Asian citizen

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer pieces surround the inner one

parts.note: a and an are both indefinite articles
F, G and H run on in order through the alphabet

explanation.surface: Grammar talk about two articles and a run of letters, oddly tied to an Asian citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: English has two indefinite articles, and they sit either side of the alphabet run; only one run of three makes a word.
explanation.definitionFit: An Afghan is a native or national of Afghanistan, a country in central Asia.

clue.text: Accountant on mad frolic gobbles one, which is fattening

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant

indicators.note: what is gobbled ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within another
mad means wild and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An accountant on a wild spree wolfs down something fattening.
explanation.walkthrough: CA, for chartered accountant, comes first; the reworked FROLIC takes in I.
explanation.definitionFit: Calorific food is high in calories, so eating much of it tends to make one put on weight.

clue.text: Engineers work around model

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the other way, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: the Royal Engineers are the REs, RE being their abbreviation
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Engineers working around a model, perhaps building a scale replica.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a scale replica for engineers, but it is a person who poses. RE is the British Army's Royal Engineers, here plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is someone who poses, as an artist's or photographer's model does.

clue.text: (& 21dn.) Clearing the shelves, pain-racked Conservation needs picking up

indicators.note: to be racked is to be stretched and wrenched on a torture frame, so these letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
C is the initial abbreviation, as for Conservative
to pick something up at the shops is to buy it

explanation.surface: Shops are being stripped bare while conservation efforts, wracked with trouble, need a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 12 across and 21 down. 'Picking up' looks like recovering, but it means purchasing.
explanation.definitionFit: Panic buying is people hoarding goods in a scare, which empties supermarket stock quickly.

clue.text: How you might make a call, but not the Weinstein way?

definitions.text: How you might make a call, but not the Weinstein way?

parts.words: How you might make a call
parts.note: surface reading: a way of phoning someone
setter's reading: Harvey Weinstein was notorious for groping, so the opposite of his approach keeps one's paws off people

explanation.walkthrough: The joke contrasts phoning without holding the handset with the disgraced film producer, who was anything but restrained.
explanation.definitionFit: A hands-free phone call uses a headset or speaker so the caller need not hold the device.

clue.text: Bulb placed over Private Eye to facilitate view

indicators.note: something placed over another covers it on both sides here, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: an onion is a bulb vegetable
a private eye is a private investigator, PI

explanation.surface: A light bulb is fixed above Private Eye magazine so readers can see it better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' suggests a lamp and 'Private Eye' the magazine this puzzle appears in; they are an onion and a detective.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion is a personal belief or judgement, which is what someone's view on a matter is.

clue.text: see 4ac.
China upset over BBC — "very out of it"

indicators.note: upset means toppled and disordered, so these letters tumble into a new arrangement
being out of it means being left out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very, the letter taken away

explanation.surface: China is cross about BBC coverage, calling it completely spaced out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but it is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate means mate. OVER loses V, and the rest is reworked with BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobber is Australian slang for a pal, the same meaning as china in rhyming slang.

clue.text: Hearty, stinking bishop, possibly VIP

parts.note: a hearty meal or welcome is a big one
Stinking Bishop is a pungent English cheese; possibly marks it as one example

explanation.surface: A jolly, smelly clergyman who might be an important person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stinking bishop' reads as an insult to a churchman, but Stinking Bishop is a soft washed-rind cheese from Gloucestershire.
explanation.definitionFit: A big cheese is informal for an important, influential person in an organisation.

clue.text: Ranting rudely at many a minister's practice

indicators.note: a ranting speaker is wild and out of control, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A government minister habitually rants rudely at people.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests rudeness is the habit; the definition is a satirical jibe at ministers' affairs, typical of Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Adultery is sex outside marriage, presented here satirically as a habit common among government politicians.

clue.text: Way Hazel, say, squeezed into scooped skirt

indicators.note: to be squeezed into a space is to be pushed inside it, so one piece goes within the other
scooping something out empties its middle, leaving only the outer shell

parts.note: only the first and last letters remain
hazel is one example of a tree, flagged by say

explanation.surface: A woman named Hazel squeezes herself into a low-cut skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazel' looks like a woman's name, but it is the nut tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A street is a road in a town, one kind of way, as in names like Appian Way.

clue.text: Her Majesty's pissed at three?

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and a drunk staggers about, so these letters reel out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The Queen is drunk by three in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her Majesty's' looks like the Queen, but Her Majesty's is a West End theatre in London; the question mark flags this definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Her Majesty's is a famous playhouse on the Haymarket in London's West End, so it is one example of a theatre.

clue.text: Cyclops picked up, put into the sack — unfair!

indicators.note: putting something into another places it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: the sack is slang for bed
the setter speaking of himself
to pick something up is to get it

explanation.surface: The setter complains of being picked up and put in a sack, an injustice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' is not a sound signal here; it simply means obtained. 'The sack' is bed, as in hitting the sack.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigoted people hold prejudiced, intolerant views, so their judgements of others are unjust.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Put on — that's the way with elderly

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
aged means old

explanation.surface: Someone is told that dressing up in a certain way suits older people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests getting dressed, but it means mounting a show.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on a play is to stage it, so a production put on has been staged.

clue.text: Exhibited by love rat and every one shafting poor Terry

indicators.note: a shaft is driven into something, so one piece is thrust inside the other
poor means in bad shape, so these letters are battered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
each means every one

explanation.surface: A cheating lover and everyone else are screwing over poor Terry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhibited by love rat' is a noun-phrase definition: the quality a cheating partner shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Treachery is betrayal of trust, the disloyalty a cheating partner displays towards the person deceived.

clue.text: Authentic boozers ruining mascara, as lacking

indicators.note: ruining something wrecks its form, so these letters are wrecked into a new order
lacking something means being without it, so some letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: Real drinkers smear their mascara.
explanation.walkthrough: CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale, a British group promoting traditional beer. MASCARA without AS leaves MCARA to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The campaign's members champion real ale, traditionally brewed beer, so they are drinkers of the genuine stuff.

clue.text: Southern seaside town with large house of ill repute

parts.note: Hove is a seaside town on England's south coast, beside Brighton
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A south-coast resort has a big brothel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House of ill repute' normally means a brothel; here it is read literally as a house with a bad reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: A hovel is a squalid, wretched dwelling, a home nobody thinks well of.

clue.text: Short member of nobility wants alternative face protection

parts.note: Vis is the short form of viscount, a rank of nobleman
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A small aristocrat wants a different kind of face mask.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like a comment on the noble's height, but it means abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: A visor is the movable front of a helmet, or a shield, that guards the face.

clue.text: Beijing's ultimate spin machine alternative? That's depressing

definitions.note: adjective for a noun answer; read with 'That's' as the state that depresses

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter
a loom weaves thread, an alternative to a spinning machine in textile making

explanation.surface: A gloomy comment on China's propaganda machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin machine' suggests propaganda, but it is a textile machine; the loom weaves rather than spins.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloom is a mood of despondency and sadness, the condition something depressing produces.

clue.text: Number associated with Boris — sense disruption by eastern state

parts.note: Boris Johnson as Prime Minister lived at Number Ten Downing Street

indicators.note: a disruption throws things into disorder, so these letters fall out of place

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
E is the abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's Downing Street brings disruption, perhaps in an eastern state.
explanation.walkthrough: Number Ten Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's official residence, so the number is TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennessee is one of the fifty United States, in the American South.

clue.text: Put down 'wicked' in Act

indicators.note: in means placed within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a deed is an act
in slang both wicked and mean are terms of praise, meaning excellent

explanation.surface: A cruel action written into an Act of Parliament is shot down.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'wicked' flag its slang sense of great, which is also what mean means in slang, as in plays a mean guitar.
explanation.definitionFit: To demean someone is to belittle or humiliate them, as a disparaging remark puts them down.

clue.text: The end of Corbyn: peer-like? Not quite

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter
an earl is a peer, so earl-y is jokingly like a peer

explanation.surface: Jeremy Corbyn's career ends with him almost, but not quite, given a peerage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of Corbyn' sounds like his political downfall; it is just his last letter. Corbyn is the former Labour leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly means almost but not fully, which is exactly what not quite expresses.
